              Energy Laws -                Laws of Thermodynamics


●   The first law of thermodynamics is the principle of the
    conservation of energy: for any physical or chemical
    change, the total amount of energy in the universe
    remains constant; energy may        change form or it may be
    transported from one region to another, but it         cannot be
    created or destroyed.

●   The second law of thermodynamics, states that the
    universe always tends toward increasing disorder: in all
    natural processes, the entropy of the universe increases.

pages.title: Thermodynamic quantities describing energy changes

pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
               Thermodynamic quantities describing energy changes



⬣    Free energy (ΔG) is the energy that can perform work during a reaction.
            - Exergonic reactions release free energy (ΔG < 0)
            - Endergonic reactions gain free energy (ΔG > 0).

⬣    Enthalpy (ΔH) is the heat content of the reacting system.
            - Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0)
            - Endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0).

⬣    Entropy (ΔS) is a measure of randomness or disorder in a system. Reactions
     with a gain in entropy involve more disordered products.

⬣    The relationship between ΔG, ΔH, and ΔS is given by the equation
                                   ΔG = ΔH –      TΔS

                  ATP as Energy Source in Metabolism

⬣    Intermediate Energy Release:

              -While compounds like PEP release more energy, ATP's intermediate release is suitable for cellular processes.
              -Releasing too much energy at once could be inefficient or harmful.

⬣    Regulation:

              -Controlled ATP hydrolysis ensures a managed and regulated energy release.
              -Tuning energy release is crucial for specific cellular activities.

⬣    Economic Considerations:

              -ATP synthesis and hydrolysis are efficiently coupled to metabolic pathways.
              -The cost of ATP synthesis and usage is reasonable, making it an economical choice for cells               .

⬣    Buffering Capacity:

              -ATP is present in high concentrations, providing a readily available energy reservoir.

           How Enzymes Work

⬣    Enzymes are biological catalysts that facilitate and
     accelerate biochemical reactions in living
     organisms.

⬣    Substrate Binding:

            - Enzymes have a specific active site for
            substrate binding.
            - The binding forms an enzyme-substrate
            complex.
            - This complex brings the reactive groups of
            the substrate(s) into proximity, facilitating
            the biochemical reaction.
            - Induced fit occurs as a result of the
            enzyme-substrate complex

                  How Enzymes Work

⬣    Catalysis of the Reaction:

            - Enzymes stabilize the transition state, lowering
            activation energy.
            - This accelerates specific biochemical reactions.

⬣    Product Formation and Release:

            - Catalyzed reactions result in product formation.
            - Products are released, and enzymes remain unchanged.
            - Enzymes are available for reuse, catalyzing multiple
            reactions.

Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
        Central Importance of Glucose

⬣   Glucose is an excellent fuel.
          – Yields good amount of energy upon oxidation
          (ΔG complete oxidation = –2840 kJ/mol)
          – Can be efficiently stored in the polymeric form
          – Many organisms and tissues can meet their
          energy needs on glucose only.

⬣   Glucose is a versatile biochemical precursor.
          – Many organisms can use glucose to generate:
            ■   All the amino   acids
            ■   Membrane      lipids
            ■   Nucleotides    inDNA   and  RNA
            ■   Cofactors   needed   for the  metabolism

pages.title: Cellular Respiration (Glucose Catabolism)
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
             Cellular Respiration (Glucose Catabolism)

  ⬣    Cellular respiration, is a multi-step process that converts glucose into energy (ATP)
       through different biochemical pathways. It consists of four main stages:

1. Glycolysis (Anaerobic Respiration)
-   Occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell.
-   Break 1 glucose molecule into 2 pyruvate molecules.
-   Produces a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH molecules.

2. Formation of Acetyl Coenzyme A
-   Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
-   Each pyruvate (C₃) is converted into acetyl-CoA (C₂)
-   Generates 2 NADH from NAD⁺.

3. Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle) –  Aerobic Process
-   Takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
-   Produces a net of 2 ATP, 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂  molecules.

4. Electron Transport Chain (ETC) -    Oxidative Phosphorylation
-   Occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
-   NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the ETC generating about 32-34 ATP per glucose.
pages.figureNotes: Figure labels: CYTOPLASM; mitochondrion; electron shuttles across membrane. Glycolysis: glucose → 2 pyruvate, +2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and 2 NADH. Pyruvate oxidation → 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 NADH. Citric acid cycle: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, +2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. Oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport and chemiosmosis): +about 28 ATP. Maximum per glucose: about 32 ATP. Cytosolic NADH shuttle labels show 2 NADH or 2 FADH2 routes. This conflicts with the bullet assigning about 32–34 ATP to ETC; both are retained, numerical claim not scored.

pages.title: Glycolysis: Importance
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                                     Glycolysis: Importance

⬣  Glycolysis is a nearly universal 10-step metabolic pathway by which a molecule of
   glucose is converted in a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions to yield two molecules
   of the three-carbon compound pyruvate
           Pyruvate can be further aerobically oxidized.
           Pyruvate can be used as a precursor in biosynthesis.

⬣  Some of the free energy is captured by the synthesis of ATP                 and NADH.

⬣  The glycolytic breakdown of glucose is the sole source of metabolic energy in some
            mammalian tissues and cell types

pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                   Glycolysis: The Preparatory Phase

⬣  In the preparatory phase of Glycolysis:

      –    Two ATP molecules are
           consumed to raise the free
           energy ∆G of the intermediates.

      –    For each molecule of glucose
           that passes through the
           preparatory phase, two
           molecules of glyceraldehyde 3-
           phosphate are formed.

pages.title: Glycolysis: The Payoff Phase
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                        Glycolysis: The Payoff Phase

⬣  The payoff phase yields:

       –    Energy is conserved in the payoff
            phase as 4 ATP molecules and 2
            NADH molecules are formed (a  net
            of 2 ATP and 2 NADH molecules)

       –    Two molecules of 1,3-
            bisphosphoglycerate are converted
            to two molecules of pyruvate.

pages.title: Noteworthy Chemical Transformations of Glycolysis
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
Noteworthy Chemical Transformations of Glycolysis

⬣   In the sequential reactions of glycolysis, three types of
    chemical transformations are particularly noteworthy:

       1.   Degradation of the carbon skeleton of glucose to yield
            pyruvate

       2.  Phosphorylation of ADP to ATP by compounds with high
           phosphoryl group transfer potential, formed during
           glycolysis

       3.   Transfer of a hydride ion to NAD+, forming NADH

pages.title: Importance of Phosphorylated Intermediates
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
           Importance of Phosphorylated Intermediates

⬣   Each of the nine glycolytic intermediates between
   glucose and pyruvate is phosphorylated. The
   phosphoryl groups have three functions.

      –    Prevent glycolytic intermediates from
           leaving the cell
      –    Serve as essential components in the
           enzymatic conservation of metabolic energy
      –    Lower the activation energy and increase
           the specificity of the enzymatic reactions

Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                              Fates         of Pyruvate

⬣    Energy stored in pyruvate can be extracted by:

      –     Aerobic processes:
             •     Oxidative reactions in the citric acid cycle
             •     Oxidative phosphorylation

      –     Anaerobic processes
             •     Reduction to lactate
             •     Reduction to ethanol

pages.title: The Role of Biotin in the Pyruvate Carboxylase Reaction
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
       The Role of Biotin in the
Pyruvate Carboxylase Reaction

 ⬣    Biotin is attached to the enzyme through an amide
      bond with the ε-amino group of a Lys residue,
      forming biotinyl-enzyme.
 ⬣     Biotin-mediated carboxylation reactions occur in
      two phases, generally catalyzed in separate active
      sites on the enzyme.
 ⬣     In the first phase (steps 1 to 3), bicarbonate is
      converted to the more activated CO2, and then used
      to carboxylate biotin.
 ⬣    The biotin acts as a carrier to transport the CO      2 from
      one active site to another on an adjacent monomer
      of the tetrameric enzyme (step 4 ).
 ⬣     In the second phase (steps 5 to 7), catalyzed in this
      second active site, the CO2 reacts with pyruvate to
      form oxaloacetate.
pages.figureNotes: Seven numbered image steps: (1) Bicarbonate is activated by ATP, forming carboxyphosphate; ATP→ADP. (2) Carboxyphosphate breaks down to CO2; Pi released. (3) CO2 reacts with biotin to form carboxybiotin; carboxybiotinyl-enzyme shown. (4) Biotin transports the CO2 from one active site to the other. (5) Biotin is decarboxylated; pyruvate is converted to its enolate form. (6) Pyruvate enolate reacts with CO2 to form oxaloacetate. (7) Oxaloacetate is released. Figure labels include adenosine, biotinyl-lysine, Lys, catalytic sites 1 and 2, pyruvate carboxylase, pyruvate enolate and oxaloacetate.

Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

Glycolysis and Gluconeogenesis Are Reciprocally
                                Regulated

⬣  Simultaneous operation of both pathways at each of the three bypass points
   would consume ATP without accomplishing chemical or biological work

⬣  Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are reciprocally regulated so that both
   processes don’t occur simultaneously in the same tissues.

⬣  Most regulatory mechanisms act on reactions that are unique to each
   pathway.

⬣  Regulation prevents wasteful operation of both pathways at the same time

pages.title: Regulation of Glycolysis
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writing agent write_glycolysis; page images inspected; not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                                 Regulation Of Glycolysis

⬣   Glycolysis is under tight regulation to ensure stable ATP
    levels

⬣   This regulation involves a sophisticated balance among ATP
    consumption, NAD regeneration, and the allosteric control
    of three key glycolytic enzymes: hexokinase, PFK-1, and
    pyruvate kinase.

⬣   Hormones such as glucagon, epinephrine, and insulin play a
    role in the regulation of glycolysis.

⬣   Additionally, the expression of genes for various glycolytic
    enzymes can be altered to exert control over glycolytic
    activity.

Pyruvate kinase converts PEP to pyruvate: fructose 1,6-bisphosphate stimulates; ATP inhibits.

     Hexokinase Isozymes Are Affected Differently
            by Their Product, Glucose 6-Phosphate

⬣  Hexokinase initiates glycolysis and found in most tissues, including muscle and brain.

⬣  Low Km (high affinity) for glucose enables glycolysis initiation even at low blood

⬣  Relatively low Vmax, limiting the rate of glucose phosphorylation.

⬣  Hexokinase I, Hexokinase II, and Hexokinase III are all inhibited by their product,
   glucose 6-phosphate (G6P), which is an important regulatory step preventing
   excessive ATP consumption when glucose is abundant.

⬣  Hexokinase IV (glucokinase) found in liver is not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate

⬣   Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a key allosteric effector for the enzymes PFK-1 and FBPase-1 in

pages.title: Cellular Respiration
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

   Cellular Respiration



⬣   Cellular respiration is a process by which the pyruvate produced
    by glycolysis is further oxidized to H2O and CO2

           - Used by animals, plants, and many microorganisms
           - Provides more energy (ATP) from glucose than glycolysis
           - Also captures energy stored in lipids and amino           acids


⬣   Occurs in three major stages       :

           - Acetyl CoA production
           - Acetyl CoA oxidation
           - Electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation

pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:

Conversion of Pyruvate to Acetyl-CoA



                                                                    ⬣   Oxidative decarboxylation of
                                                                        pyruvate is an irreversible
                                                                        oxidation process in which the
                                                                        carboxyl group is removed,
                                                                        forming CO2 and acetyl-CoA


                                                                    ⬣   Catalyzed by the pyruvate
                                                                        dehydrogenase complex


                                                                    ⬣   Requires five cofactors, four of
                                                                        which are derived from vitamins.

pages.title: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDH)
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
           Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDH)


⬣   The PDH is a large multienzyme       Complex Employs Three Enzymes and Five
    Coenzymes to Oxidize Pyruvate


⬣   Contains multiple copies of three enzymes
          - Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)
          - Dihydrolipoyl   transacetylase   (E2)
          - Dihydrolipoyl   dehydrogenase (E3)


⬣   Requires five different coenzymes or prosthetic groups
          - Lipoate  (lipoicacid)
          - Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) derived from vitamin (B1)
          - Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) derived from vitamin (B2)
          - Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) derived from vitamin (B3)
          - Coenzyme A (CoA, CoA-SH) derived from vitamin (B5)

Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
   Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by the PDH complex

⬣   Enzyme 1
    Step 1: Decarboxylation of pyruvate to the
    hydroxyethyl derivative
    Step 2: Oxidation of the hydroxyethyl derivative to
    an acetyl group
            ‒ Electrons and the acetyl group are
transferred from TPP to the lipoyllysyl   group of E2

⬣   Enzyme 2
   Step 3: Formation of acetyl-CoA (product 1)

⬣   Enzyme 3
    Step 4: Electron transfer to regenerate the oxidized
    form of the lipoyllysyl  group

   Step 5: Regeneration of the oxidized FAD cofactor
            ‒ Forming NADH (product 2)

pages.title: Regulation of Pyruvate dehydrogenase Complex
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
            Regulation of Pyruvate dehydrogenase Complex


⬣   The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) is regulated through a combination of covalent
    modification and allosteric mechanisms


⬣   The PDH complex in mammals is allosterically inhibited by ATP, acetyl-CoA, and NADH


⬣    AMP, CoA, and NAD+, which accumulate when acetate flow into the citric acid cycle is
    insufficient, allosterically  activates the PDH complex      .


⬣   High levels of ATP and NADH, indicative of sufficient energy production, inhibit the PDH
    complex, slowing down pyruvate decarboxylation            .


⬣   Elevated levels of ADP and calcium ions activate the complex, promoting the conversion of
    pyruvate to acetyl   -CoA when more energy is needed

pages.title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency


    ⬣   Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency is a rare genetic mitochondrial disorder that
        results from mutations in the genes encoding components of the PDH complex,
        leading to a dysfunctional enzyme.


    ⬣   PDH deficiency is most commonly linked to the alpha unit of E1, which is X-linked,
        but autosomal recessive variants also exist.


    ⬣   It causes elevated serum lactate, pyruvate and alanine.


    ⬣   Associated with lactic acidosis, progressive neurological and neuromuscular
        degeneration, and, usually, death during childhood.

pages.title: Therapeutic Approaches for PDH Deficiency
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

Therapeutic Approaches for PDH Deficiency


⬣   Use of a ketogenic diet:

          - High-fat, adequate protein, low-carb diet.
          - Forces the body to prioritize fat metabolism.
          - Mitigates metabolic challenges in PDH Deficiency.


⬣   Dichloroacetic    Acid (DCA):

          - Investigated for treating lactic acidosis in PDH Deficiency.
          - Stimulates pyruvate dehydrogenase activity.
          - Inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase.
          - Shifts metabolism toward mitochondrial oxidation,
          reducing lactate production.

pages.title: Thiamin (Vitamin B1) deficiency causes Beriberi
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

Thiamin (Vitamin B1) deficiency causes Beriberi



  ⬣   Thiamine is an essential dietary requirement for most vertebrates.


  ⬣   Most vertebrates do not synthesize or store thiamine in significant amounts.


  ⬣   Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) serves as a crucial coenzyme for the pyruvate
      dehydrogenase complex (PDH) in glucose metabolism.


  ⬣   Thiamine deficiency leads to Beriberi, a fatal disease, that is characterized by neurological
      disturbances, paralysis, limb atrophy, and cardiac failure.


  ⬣   Beriberi is rare in developed countries due to vitamin-enriched foods. It is more prevalent in
      individuals who abuse alcohol, as excess alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and storage,
      leading to poor nutrition.

pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
topics: Reactions of the Citric Acid Cycle
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
           Reactions of the
            Citric Acid Cycle


⬣   In each cycle turn, one acetyl group enters
    as acetyl-CoA, and two molecules of CO2
    are released.

⬣   One molecule of oxaloacetate is used to
    form citrate, and one is regenerated.


⬣   Four of the eight steps involve oxidations,
    conserving energy in the form of NADH
    and FADH2.

⬣   NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the
    respiratory chain, driving ATP synthesis.
pages.visualNotes: Full labeled cycle: 1 aldol condensation; 2a dehydration and 2b rehydration reposition citrate OH in isocitrate to set up next decarboxylation; 3 oxidative decarboxylation, OH oxidized to carbonyl and CO2 lost; 4 oxidative decarboxylation with PDH-like mechanism dependent on carbonyl on adjacent carbon; 5 substrate-level phosphorylation, thioester energy conserved in GTP/ATP phosphoanhydride; 6 dehydrogenation introduces double bond and initiates methylene oxidation sequence; 7 hydration introduces OH for next oxidation; 8 OH dehydrogenation gives carbonyl positioned for aldol condensation. NADH at isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate and malate steps; FADH2 at succinate step; GTP/ATP at succinyl-CoA step; two CO2 at steps3 and4; CoA-SH at step1 and5; CoA-SH entry at step4.

Formation of Citrate



  ⬣   Citrate synthase catalyzes the condensation of acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate
             - Involves the formation of a transient intermediate, citroyl-CoA
             - Large, negative ∆G′°    is needed because [oxaloacetate] is normally very low

Induced Fit in the Citrate Synthase



 ⬣    Binding of oxaloacetate causes a conformational
      change creating a binding site for acetyl-CoA


        ○    Open conformation:
             Free enzyme does not have a binding site for
             acetyl-CoA.
        ○    Closed conformation:
             Binding of OAA creates binding for acetyl-CoA.


 ⬣    Induced fit decreases the likelihood of premature
      cleavage of the thioester bond of acetyl-CoA

Net Result of the Citric Acid Cycle



 ⬣   Net oxidation of two carbons to CO2


 ⬣   The energy released by oxidation is
     conserved in the production of:


    3 NADH
    1 FADH2


 ⬣   Generates 1 GTP, which can be
     converted to ATP

2CO2 + 3NADH + FADH2 + GTP + CoA + 3H+

pages.title: Summary
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
                           Summary



⬣   Acetyl-CoA initiates the cycle by donating its acetyl group to oxaloacetate, forming citrate, a six-carbon
    compound.
⬣   Citrate is converted into isocitrate, another six-carbon molecule. Dehydrogenation of isocitrate, with
    the loss of CO2, produces α-ketoglutarate, a five-carbon compound.
⬣   α-Ketoglutarate     undergoes further decarboxylation, losing a second CO2 molecule, ultimately yielding
    succinate, a four-carbon compound.
⬣   Succinate is enzymatically converted in three steps into oxaloacetate, completing the cycle.
⬣   Each cycle turnover involves the entry of one acetyl group (two carbons) from acetyl-CoA. Two
    molecules of CO2 are released. One molecule of oxaloacetate is used to form citrate, and one molecule
    is regenerated, ensuring no net removal of oxaloacetate.
⬣   Four of the eight steps in the cycle are oxidation reactions, leading to the efficient conservation of
    energy in the form of reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2.
⬣   Oxaloacetate is present in cells in very low concentrations, allowing it theoretically to participate in the
    oxidation of numerous acetyl groups.
pages.visualNotes: The summary restates one acetyl group/two CO2 per turnover, four oxidation reactions of eight steps conserving NADH/FADH2, and very low cellular OAA permitting repeated acetyl-group oxidation.

pages.title: Role of the Citric Acid Cycle in Anabolism
pages.visualReviewer: Codex chapter writer; source inspection, not independent review
topics: Role of the Citric Acid Cycle in Anabolism
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
     Role of the Citric Acid
     Cycle in Anabolism


⬣   The citric acid cycle serves both catabolic and
    anabolic processes in aerobic organisms.


⬣   Oxaloacetate and α-ketoglutarate       serve as
    precursors for aspartate and glutamate
    through simple transamination.


⬣   Succinyl-CoA, is crucial for synthesizing the
    porphyrin ring of heme     groups.

⬣   Oxaloacetate from the cycle can be
    converted to glucose through
    gluconeogenesis.

Red replenishing arrows: pyruvate → OAA (pyruvate carboxylase), PEP → OAA (PEP carboxylase), pyruvate → malate (malic enzyme).

                      Anaplerotic                Reactions


⬣    Intermediates in the citric acid cycle can be used in biosynthetic pathways (removed from cycle).

⬣    Must replenish the intermediates in order for          the cycle and central metabolic pathway to          continue


⬣    The most important anaplerotic        reaction in mammalian liver, kidney, and brown adipose tissue is
     the reversible carboxylation of pyruvate        to form oxaloacetate, catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

   Citric Acid Cycle Regulation



⬣   Regulation balances the supply of key
    intermediates with the demands of energy
    production and biosynthetic processes


⬣   Regulation occurs at several points:

          - PDH complex
          - Citrate synthase
          - Isocitrate dehydrogenase complex

Energy from Reduced Fuels Is Used to Synthesize
ATP in Animals


 ⬣    Carbohydrates, lipids, and amino
      acids are the main reduced fuels
      for the cell.

 ⬣    Electrons from reduced fuels are
      transferred to reduced cofactors
      NADH or FADH2.

 ⬣    Oxidative phosphorylation
      occurs in mitochondria, where
      the energy from NADH and
      FADH2 is used to make ATP.

pages.title: Structure of a mitochondrion
pages.visualReviewer: Codex parent agent (source preparation, not activity review)
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025

              Structure of a Mitochondrion


⬣    Outer membrane
            – Relatively porous membrane; allows passage of metabolites

⬣    Inner membrane
            – Relatively impermeable, with proton gradient across it
            – Location of electron transport chain complexes
            – Convolutions called cristae serve to increase the surface area.

⬣    Intermembrane space (IMS)
            - Similar environment to cytosol
            - Higher proton concentration ( lower pH)
⬣    Matrix
            – Location of the citric acid cycle and parts of lipid and amino acid
            metabolism
            – Lower proton concentration (higher pH)
pages.figureAndTableDetails: Figure labels: outer membrane freely permeable to small molecules and ions; inner membrane impermeable to most small molecules and ions, including H+. Inner membrane contains respiratory electron carriers (Complexes I–IV), ADP–ATP translocase, ATP synthase (FoF1), other membrane transporters. Cristae, ribosomes, porin channels. Matrix contains pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, citric acid cycle enzymes, fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, amino acid oxidation enzymes, DNA, ribosomes, many other enzymes, ATP, ADP, Pi, Mg2+, Ca2+, K+, many soluble metabolic intermediates.

pages.title: Universal electron acceptors
pages.visualReviewer: Codex parent agent (source preparation, not activity review)
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
Electrons Are Funneled to Universal Electron Acceptors

              ⬣    Dehydrogenases collect electrons from catabolic pathways and funnel them into
                   universal electron acceptors:

              1- Nicotinamide nucleotides (NAD+ or NADP+)
                     - Catalyze reversible reactions of the general type:
                     reduced substrate + NAD+        ⇄   oxidized substrate + NADH + H+
                     - Two hydrogen atoms are removed from the substrates:
                                One is transferred as a hydride ion (:H-) to NAD(P)+
                                One is released as H+ in the medium

              2- Flavin nucleotides (FMN or FAD)
                      -The oxidized flavin   nucleotide can accept either:
                         One electron (yielding the semiquinone        form) or
                         Two electrons (yielding FADH2 or FMNH2)

pages.visualReviewer: Codex parent agent (source preparation, not activity review)
pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
Electrons –              carrying molecules of the Respiratory chain

              ⬣    Oxidative phosphorylation begins with the entry of electrons into the series of electron
                   carriers called the respiratory chain

              ⬣    Three types of electron transfers occur in oxidative phosphorylation:

                           - Direct transfer of electrons
                           -Transfer as a hydrogen atom (H+ + e−)
                           -Transfer as a hydride ion (:H−), which bears two electrons.

              ⬣    The respiratory chain contains five types of electron-carrying molecules

                      -    Nicotinamide nucleotide (NAD+       or NADP+)
                      -    Flavin nucleotide or Flavoproteins      (FMN or FAD)
                      -    Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q or Q)
                      -    Cytochromes
                      -    Iron-sulfur proteins

               The Malate-Aspartate Shuttle


⬣    The NADH dehydrogenase of the inner
     mitochondrial membrane accepts electrons

pages.text:
Dr. Osama Essawi 2025
     Oxidative Phosphorylation Is Regulated by Cellular
                                                Energy Needs



⬣    The rate of O₂ consumption in mitochondria is regulated by ADP availability (acceptor control of respiration).

⬣    Cellular energy status is indicated by intracellular ADP concentration and the           [ATP]/[ADP]·[Pi ]  “mass-action
     ratio” (which is typically high  ).

⬣    When energy demand increases (e.g., during protein synthesis), ATP is broken down to ADP + Pi, lowering the
     mass-action ratio.

⬣    Increased ADP availability stimulates oxidative phosphorylation, leading to higher respiration rates and ATP
     regeneration.

⬣    This cycle ensures a stable ATP supply, matching ATP formation to consumption, maintaining cellular energy
     balance.
